Our proposed approach, called Resilient Decentralized Stochastic Projected Gradient with Dynamic Communication (RDS-PGD-DC), enables non-malicious agents to adapt their communication links dynamically while minimizing the impact of interference from malicious agents. Our key finding is that RDS-PGD-DC converges to an optimal solution under certain conditions, even when communication links are dynamically adjusted and communication noise is present. Our research also includes the development of a new metric to evaluate the effectiveness of dynamic communication management, as well as the demonstration of the approach's effectiveness in solving a non-linear optimization problem with missing data.

We have developed a Python-based toolkit to accurately replicate the impact of instrumental systematic effects on future wide-field, multi-object spectrographs. By creating realistic mock data that includes realistic effects like pixel-to-pixel variations, wavelength calibration errors, and fiber crosstalk, we can generate training datasets for machine learning algorithms. This approach allows us to develop and refine methods for correcting these systematic biases, ultimately leading to more precise cosmological observations.

Our study focuses on partial tree linearization, a task that involves determining the order of children nodes in a given partial tree structure. We utilize the existing word ordering dataset from Universal Dependencies, which is suitable for this purpose. Our findings reveal that performance in partial tree linearization is closely tied to the prevalence of right-branching patterns in the data. We also found that the BART model's effectiveness declines when applied to partial tree linearization, as opposed to word ordering, due to its tendency to generate highly right-branching structures.

Our research focuses on developing a novel neural network architecture called MDDNet, designed to detect deepfakes across various platforms. To address the issue of domain shifts, we incorporate three types of connections into the network: adaptive instance normalization connections, cross-domain knowledge connections, and cross-task knowledge connections, all of which are cross-stitch connections. These connections enable the network to adapt to different domains and tasks by learning shared and task-specific feature extractors. Specifically, our network learns adaptive instance normalization connections to handle domain shifts in input data, cross-domain knowledge connections to transfer knowledge across different domains, and cross-task knowledge connections to transfer knowledge across different tasks. Our approach has been tested on multiple datasets, including Face2Face, Deepfake, and Omega, and has shown superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our results demonstrate that our network can effectively detect deepfakes across various platforms by leveraging its ability to adapt to different domains and tasks.

We adapt the angle function concept from Euclidean space to real-valued angle functions on a unit sphere associated with two distinct smooth directions in a differentiable different space. Our main finding is that our generalized angle function can be used to determine whether different space admits a conformal mapping to different power of itself. Specifically, our novel angle function helps prove that different space cannot be conformally mapped to its square, and this result extends to cases where different space contains an isometrically embedded parabolic substructure. Our results also imply that different space cannot be conformally mapped to its square in cases where different space contains an isometrically embedded substructure with specific angle function properties.

We establish inequalities between isomorphism classes of orders within number fields, utilizing the Stickelberger ideal and its applications. Specifically, we determine conditions under which inequalities of the form $[	ext{1 } \text{ $\text{ll}_{\text{S}}$ } \text{ $\lambda_1$ }^{f_1} \text{ ... } \text{ $\lambda_{n-1}$ }^{f_{n-1}}$ ]$ hold, where $\text{S}$ represents the set of infinite primes of a number field, $\text{ $\lambda_i$ }$ are Lagrange bases, and $\text{ $f_i$ }$ are positive integers. These inequalities are influenced by class numbers, fundamental units, and regulators of number fields, and we demonstrate how they can be employed to compare isomorphism classes of orders and solve specific Diophantine equations.

We establish that the quantum group's basis, denoted as $\bar{\mathfrak{\theta}}$, remains unchanged under the action of the braid group and Dynkin's automorphisms, which were initially proposed by Lusztig. This is in contrast to the quantum group's canonical and dual canonical bases, which only partially maintain their structure after undergoing the action of these transformations. As a result, the images of the canonical and dual canonical bases under these actions can be expressed as linear combinations of the $\bar{\mathfrak{\theta}}$ basis, with non-negative integer coefficients. These findings can be viewed as an extension of the established properties of the BZ basis within the framework of the negative part of the quantum group.

A 2020 news report highlighted the tragic consequences of a cryptocurrency pyramid scheme called Forsage, which led to the suicides of two of its participants. This incident is not unique, as Forsage has been identified as a deceptive platform that has caused financial harm to the vast majority of its users, with only a tiny fraction profiting from it. Our research expands on this issue by developing a mathematical model that simulates the dynamics of pyramid schemes, taking into account the varying levels of investment and the limited time available for participants to recoup their losses. Our model reveals that the majority of participants will experience losses, regardless of the specific rules governing the scheme. Furthermore, our research shows that the proportion of participants who lose money increases as the rate at which new participants join the scheme slows down. Our findings also have implications for the stability of cryptocurrencies that rely on similar deceptive practices.

A study examined the properties of 11 potential globular clusters in the Milky Way, identified through data from the Gaia DR2 mission. By analyzing the color and brightness of 1,000 stars within each cluster's area, researchers used isochrones to determine the clusters' ages, distances, and densities. The results showed that these clusters are relatively young, with ages ranging from 100 million to 9 billion years, and are located between 3.5 and 20 kiloparsecs from the galactic center. The study's findings are valuable for understanding the formation and development of star clusters in the galactic bulge.

We investigate tensor networks that use a single type of tensor acting as a quantum state, and which can perform the task of correcting lost information through the network. We establish the conditions under which a tensor network correction protocol is feasible, and demonstrate that any such network with correctability properties must have a specific structure, and that the protocol itself must also adhere to particular constraints. We also examine the implications of our findings for TOSNet, a recently developed and highly efficient tensor network that exhibits correctability properties.

In sequential decision-making processes, the outcome of each step influences the subsequent outcomes, making it crucial to accurately predict the results of future steps. This is particularly relevant in business processes, where the outcome of a specific task can impact the outcomes of other tasks. To address this challenge, researchers have developed various methods, including tree-based models, neural networks, and matrix factorization techniques. However, these methods often overlook the inherent structure of business processes. To overcome this limitation, a novel graph-based approach has been proposed, which captures the complex relationships between tasks in a business process. This approach employs a graph neural network to predict task outcomes, and its performance has been evaluated on real-world datasets, demonstrating its superiority over existing methods. Furthermore, the approach has been extended to handle multi-label prediction scenarios, where a single instance can belong to multiple categories.

This paper investigates the behavior of functions whose Fourier transforms have growth rates that are influenced by either polynomial or exponential factors. We establish a relationship between the polynomial or exponential growth rates of a function and its corresponding derivatives in time and space. Specifically, we derive growth estimates that are self-consistent for functions in Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are defined by their growth rates in both time and space. Our results are expressed as inequalities that bound the functions and their derivatives, taking into account the consistency of growth rates. Our approach involves utilizing the Paley-Wiener theorem and the properties of analytic functions in complex domains.

We conducted an in-depth analysis of the hydrogen line width in the solar spectrum during a significant X-class flare, specifically F22.62X2, on December 14, 2022. By examining the line width evolution, we aimed to understand the physical conditions of the solar atmosphere during the event. Our study revealed that the line width changes were primarily driven by temperature variations rather than turbulent velocities. We found that the line width in the near-ultraviolet spectrum closely mirrored the temperature changes, whereas the far-ultraviolet line width was more sensitive to high-temperature components. Interestingly, we observed that the line width in the extreme ultraviolet spectrum was primarily determined by Doppler broadening caused by high-temperature plasma, rather than velocity fields. Our findings also indicated that the line width in the near-ultraviolet spectrum could serve as a reliable indicator of the solar atmosphere's temperature, particularly in the pre-flare and post-flare phases. We believe that monitoring the line width in the hydrogen line spectrum could provide valuable insights into the solar atmosphere's physical conditions and help predict the occurrence of solar flares.

Deep learning models' vulnerability to adversarial examples is a significant concern, especially when it comes to robustness against transformations. Current research has focused on geometric transformations like rotations and scaling, neglecting more complex point cloud transformations. We introduce a novel framework, TPC, to assess and enhance robustness against arbitrary geometric transformations in point cloud data. Our framework defines a new category of transformation called "twisting," which combines rotation and translation, and develops a loss function to guide model training. Experimental results demonstrate that TPC significantly reduces misclassification rates under twisting transformations compared to existing methods. Furthermore, our framework provides insights into the types of transformations that a model is most vulnerable to, offering a more comprehensive understanding of model robustness.

Our study focuses on the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, examining its pole positions through a range of theoretical models within the RPA framework. By utilizing a Gaussian expansion method to describe the spatial distribution of $^{16}$O, we calculated the resonance's pole positions within the RPA framework. Our calculations revealed pole positions at 31.8 MeV and 32.4 MeV, which were found to be in close agreement with experimental data. Furthermore, we examined the influence of different approaches to modeling the two-body currents on the pole positions, finding that the inclusion of relativistic currents resulted in a slight shift towards lower energy compared to non-relativistic currents.

Non-linear dynamical systems often exhibit complex dynamics that are difficult to model and predict. The Koopman operator framework provides a useful tool for analyzing these systems by representing them in a linear setting through the use of nonlinear functions of state variables. Despite its benefits, estimating the Koopman operator from observed time-series data can be computationally expensive, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional data. We introduce a novel approach to Koopman operator estimation that significantly reduces computational costs by employing a sparse approximation of the underlying dictionary used in our method. This approach is demonstrated through numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, including the Lorenz-96 model and atmospheric pressure data from the Mauna Loa observatory.

To address the issue of neural text generation's inability to capture long-range dependencies, we propose a novel approach called SparseGAN that combines generative adversarial networks with sparse attention mechanisms. Our method's architecture is composed of two sparse attention modules, one in each generator and discriminator, which dynamically allocate resources to capture both short and long-range dependencies in generated text. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments on three text generation tasks, including character, word, and sentence-level generation, and achieved state-of-the-art results in character and word generation, as well as comparable performance in sentence generation. Our findings demonstrate that SparseGAN is an effective framework for modeling complex data distributions by simultaneously capturing short and long-range dependencies in generated text.

The concept of interstellar panspermia, which involves the transfer of life between galaxies through the movement of stars, is a fascinating hypothesis. However, the extreme conditions surrounding stars, such as intense radiation and gravitational forces, pose significant challenges to the survival of living organisms. To overcome this obstacle, we propose a novel approach that focuses on identifying stellar environments with milder conditions, thereby increasing the likelihood of interstellar panspermia. By utilizing the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, we have determined that specific types of binary and triple star systems, including wide binary and triple systems, offer ideal conditions for the transfer of life. These systems, which encompass a wide range of configurations, provide a diverse array of possibilities for the interstellar transfer of organisms. The proposed framework for evaluating the feasibility of interstellar panspermia is not limited to binary and triple star systems, but can be applied to more complex multi-star systems as well.

This study introduces a novel method for estimating animal population density using data from camera traps and individual identification based solely on partial captures. We propose a modification to the existing spatial capture-recapture (SCR) model, which accounts for the possibility that animals may not be centered within the study area. Our approach involves creating an extended individual activity center for each captured animal and developing a probability model for capture based on detected cameras. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a simulation study and apply it to analyze a red fox population in an urban environment.

This study introduces a straightforward method to assess the stability of states within multilayer networks, which are composed of interconnected layers that can either be fully or partially connected to one another. By utilizing a matrix that captures the relationships between the network's layers, we can determine which layers contribute to the positive or negative feedback mechanisms present in the network. This feedback mechanism analysis allows us to verify the stability of a given network state by examining the properties of the contribution matrix. Furthermore, we can identify the independent subnetworks that make up the multilayer structure, which can be used to simplify the analysis of complex networks. Overall, our approach provides a powerful tool for understanding the dynamics of multilayer networks and can be applied to a wide range of real-world systems, including networks of coupled maps, neural networks, and networks of oscillators.

Given two differential module structures, $M$ over a field $K$ and $N$ over an extension field $L$ of $K$, along with associated differential modules $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{N}$ over the ring of differential operators $D_K$ and $D_L$ respectively, we define an operator $N$ to be dominated by $M$ if there exists a non-zero mapping from $\mathcal{M}$ to $\mathcal{N}$, and $N$ to be parametrized by $M$ if this mapping is surjective. In this paper, we introduce an algorithm to determine if $N$ is dominated by $M$, and if so, provide the mapping, or conclude that it is not dominated. Additionally, we offer an improved version of this algorithm with specific conditions met.

This work presents a novel, self-contained system designed to locate and correct bugs within programming code through an interactive process. The framework operates within a comprehensive testing environment, utilizing a combination of automated and manual methods to pinpoint errors in the codebase. The system's workflow is fully documented and includes the development of a sophisticated, cloud-based testing environment that facilitates seamless collaboration among team members. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through the correction of errors in existing research code, as well as in popular machine learning libraries. By making the code, codebase, and code correctors publicly available, this work serves as a valuable resource for others to build upon and improve the automated code correction process.

For Lie algebras of types $A_l$ and $D_l$, we define a specific ordering on their roots using the maximal root as the highest element. This new root ordering allows us to establish a correspondence between certain monomials in the Chevalley generators and a basis of the coordinate ring of the corresponding group. This basis, which we term the double Grobner basis, is constructed by monomials that are greater than the maximal root and is shown to be in correspondence with the coordinate ring's basis derived from regular functions on the Borel and unipotent varieties. This achievement is made possible through the application of double Yangians and their special sub-Yanians.

This research introduces a novel size-estimation algorithm for a single data stream within a dynamic directed graph, where the method is both distributed and deterministic, requiring only constant memory. The proposed method is specifically optimized for sparse networks, using an approach that relies on the network's second largest eigenvalue, and can also function effectively without this value by providing a looser estimation. The project's code is publicly available on GitHub.

This paper introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate the length of a queue in a single-server queueing system, where interarrival and service times are independent and follow unknown continuous distributions. The proposed method relies on the assumption that service times adhere to a stochastic ordering pattern, specifically the likelihood ratio ordering. The accuracy of the nonparametric estimator is compared to a parametric one, and a simulation study is conducted to evaluate their performance. The results demonstrate that the nonparametric estimator is more precise than the parametric one when the stochastic ordering pattern of service times is strong, but less accurate when this ordering pattern is weak.

We present a novel numerical approach to solving the Hamiltonian constraint in the context of general relativity, where we treat the metric as composed of a conformal factor and a traceless conformal part, which are handled independently. By separating the Hamiltonian constraint into its homogeneous and nonlinear components, we can express them in terms of the conformal factor's Laplacian and a residual term. This allows us to handle the conformal factor independently from the residual term, which is then used to update the Hamiltonian constraint in an iterative manner. We test our scheme using Bowen-York initial data, which yields satisfactory results.

Antiferromagnetic antiperovskite compounds are emerging as a promising platform for exploring the anomalous Nernst effect. This effect is influenced by the magnetic structure and can be manipulated to develop novel spintronic devices. In this study, we investigate the anomalous Nernst coefficient in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Co$_3$MnN using first-principles calculations. We find that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is significantly affected by the magnetic structure, with a 10-fold increase observed in the ferromagnetic state compared to the Type-II antiferromagnetic state. We also examine the impact of Mn site disorder on the anomalous Nernst coefficient, which is found to be minimal. Furthermore, we analyze the temperature dependence of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and find that it is primarily determined by the density of states near the Fermi level. Our results provide valuable insights into the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites and highlight the importance of considering temperature effects in first-principles calculations.

User facilities, such as synchrotron light sources, drive the development of experimental techniques used to investigate materials. These advancements often benefit conventional laboratories, yet the development process is rarely acknowledged or studied. To address this gap, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of material characterization techniques presented at the 2019 Synchrotron User Proposal Meetings held at three major synchrotron locations. By examining these presentations, we identified emerging techniques developed through collaboration with user facilities and tracked their progression from initial conception to widespread adoption. Our findings were synthesized into a dynamic visualization that highlights the progression of these techniques across the different synchrotron locations.

This research paper delves into non-autonomous obstacle problem where the operator is defined as the p(x)-Laplacian. It is shown that if the obstacle has a specific Sobolev regularity, then the solution shares this regularity. Furthermore, if the obstacle's gradient is of a lower Sobolev regularity, then the solution's gradient will also be of a similar regularity. The results are demonstrated under the condition of the p(x) function being bounded and having a limited oscillation.

We investigate the mod p reduction of certain crystalline extensions within the context of p-adic Hodge theory, specifically focusing on extensions of the residue field of Cp by Zp with coefficients in the continuous dual of the Galois group's dual. Our analysis involves examining the local Langlands correspondence for GL2(Zp) and its reduction modulo p, and we demonstrate that G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles are not present in the dual of the Galois group's dual for a sufficiently large p, whereas we show that crystalline cocycles do appear under specific conditions. Our findings contribute to the understanding of mod p reduction of crystalline extensions and have implications for the study of elliptic curves and their rational points.

In this paper, we introduce and investigate the notion of mesoscale flatness within the context of hypersurfaces characterized by bounded mean curvature. Our approach builds on a previously established framework for mesoscale properties, which we adapt to the hypersurface setting. We demonstrate that hypersurfaces with mean curvature that falls within a specific range exhibit mesoscale flatness, a property that holds true across varying scales. Furthermore, we show that these hypersurfaces display a form of uniform mesoscale flatness, a condition that is essential for the application of harmonic analysis techniques.

This study proposes a novel method for identifying and locating damage in self-sensing composite materials. The approach involves a two-step process, with the initial step using a finite element model to establish a relationship between material damage and sensor data. The second step determines the specific pattern of damage that best matches the recorded sensor data. The first step is made computationally efficient by employing a reduced order modeling technique, specifically the proper orthogonal decomposition method, to create a computationally lightweight model. The second step involves a computational search for the damage pattern, utilizing a genetic algorithm. The proposed methodology is validated through laboratory experiments involving the creation of artificial damage in a composite beam, with the results demonstrating the model's ability to accurately predict the location and extent of damage. The study also highlights the computational benefits of the reduced order model, which is found to be significantly faster than the full finite element model. The proposed approach is found to be particularly beneficial for identifying complex damage patterns, as it can account for their non-linear characteristics.

The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model is modified to incorporate various forms of intelligence, and the resulting model's dynamics are analyzed. The model's equations are adjusted to reflect the impact of different intelligence types, and the conditions for predator and prey co-existence or extinction are determined through stability analysis. The findings reveal that cooperative intelligence among predators can lead to their extinction, while deceptive intelligence among predators can cause their co-existence with prey. Conversely, deceptive prey can lead to their dominance over predators, and cooperative prey can result in their extinction. The model's implications are further explored through numerical simulations and discussions on the broader significance of intelligence in ecological systems.

This paper introduces a novel method for establishing integral identities using geometric vectors, which can also yield explicit formulas and potentially discover new identities. The approach is demonstrated by re-deriving a formula originally presented by Srivastava and Tomovski, as well as establishing a new integral formula that generalizes the work of Srivastava and Tomovski.

The muon g-2 anomaly measurement at Fermilab is expected to reach a precision of approximately 0.2 parts per million, which is about half the current precision. To further reduce uncertainty and explore a wider range of the relevant parameter space, particularly in the case of the contact interaction, a significant increase in the number of running muons is necessary. We propose that the muon g-2 experiment can be conducted simultaneously with the muon-to-electron conversion search at the Mu2e facility at Fermilab by utilizing the unused beamline from Mu2e to inject a fraction of the muon beam into the g-2 storage ring. This approach would enable the simultaneous execution of both experiments and significantly reduce the time required to achieve the desired precision for the muon g-2 measurement. However, the feasibility of this proposal is subject to the availability of the beamline and the development of suitable injection and extraction techniques.
We establish the spin-three Ward identities in the Toda conformal field theory using the approach developed by Delduc, Snider and West, which reveals the higher-spin symmetry inherent in the theory.

We establish that uniform lattices within the class of p-adic analytic groups possess the property of being biautomatic. This achievement is made possible by developing a family of coordinate systems tailored to specific congruence subgroups, which are shown to provide automatic structures.

Our research focuses on developing a high-precision model for predicting walking functions using ECoG signals from the motor cortex. We propose a novel approach that combines complex networks with long short-term memory, known as the CCLSTM model. To enhance the CCLSTM model's performance, we incorporate an attention mechanism and a complex network component. The attention mechanism helps identify the most relevant time steps, while the complex network component extracts key features from the input data. We conducted experiments comparing our CCLSTM model with traditional EEG decoding methods, including the LSTM model, and found that our approach outperformed the others in terms of prediction accuracy. Specifically, our model achieved an average root mean square error of 0.105 speed steps and an average correlation coefficient of 0.71, which were significant improvements over the traditional EEG decoding methods.

We demonstrate that right-angled Artin groups $A\Gamma$ possess actions on trees with specific stabilizers being isomorphic to subgroups $A\Gamma_x$ associated with vertices of a given graph, provided the graph contains at least one edge. These actions are characterized as being of "combinatorial finite asymptotic width" type. Specifically, subgroups corresponding to vertex cuts defined by connected components of the graph's complement have isomorphic stability within the group. We establish that $A\Gamma$ can be represented as having a tree action of "combinatorial finite asymptotic width" type, where individual vertex stabilizers have isomorphic isomorphism types.

Dynamic graphs, characterized by evolving structures and edge attributes over time, pose significant challenges in machine learning applications. Traditional methods typically rely on temporal aggregation to analyze local neighborhoods, neglecting the global dynamics that are crucial for understanding complex systems. To address this limitation, we present DECENNT, a novel model that simultaneously captures both local and global dynamics within a shared latent space. DECENNT employs a hierarchical framework, where an ensemble of small neural networks represents the ensemble dimension, and a gating mechanism controls the flow of information between the ensemble and mean dimensions. This design enables efficient and scalable training, with each small neural network being independently trainable. DECENNT demonstrates superior performance in node classification tasks across various dynamic graph datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods while maintaining computational efficiency.

Understanding the motion of biological entities is a fundamental aspect of biology research. However, differentiating between biological and non-biological objects in motion tracking can be a challenging task. We propose a novel method to distinguish between biological and non-biological objects in motion tracking videos. Our approach involves a two-step process: first, we detect and track objects in motion using DeepSORT, and then we classify each object as biological or non-biological using a Random Forest classifier trained on motion features extracted from DeepSAD. We also introduce a new dataset called BioMotion, consisting of 1000 video clips with moving biological and non-biological objects. Our method achieves an accuracy of 84.5% in classifying objects in motion tracking videos.

We introduce a new method for solving the Neumann problem in nested domains, combining the Nested Neumann algorithm with a novel metric known as inception depth. This metric is used to determine when to apply Neumann or Dirichlet updates in order to efficiently reduce the Neumann component of a function. Our approach is particularly effective for domains with a high aspect ratio, but we found that it converges slowly for domains with low aspect ratios. To address this issue, we developed a strategy to reduce the inception depth, which involves creating a bridge between the nested domains and modifying the metric to account for this bridge. Our results show that this strategy significantly improves the convergence rate of our algorithm, especially for domains with an aspect ratio of less than 10.

The topological properties of an Anderson insulator, which is affected by disorder, are difficult to characterize due to their dynamic nature. We develop a method to identify these topological features in the energy spectrum of a 2D Anderson insulator using a quantum walk model. By applying this approach to a quantum walk with random diagonal elements, we find that the topological markers, specifically the winding number and Zak phase, can be preserved even in the presence of disorder. We also demonstrate that these topological properties remain stable under certain types of random perturbations, such as those that maintain the symmetry of the Hamiltonian's Hamiltonian matrix. Our findings suggest that the relationship between the topological and non-topological regions of the energy spectrum can be used to detect the topological nature of the Anderson insulator, which can be experimentally verified by measuring the system's response to random perturbations.

We investigate the genus-one curve invariants proposed by Bostan, Schost, and Zvonar\'{e}v from a geometric perspective, specifically whether these invariants represent independent geometric properties. Our analysis reveals that these invariants are indeed independent geometric properties, as they remain unchanged regardless of the two points chosen to define the curve's group law. Our proof involves explicitly describing the genus-one curve and its associated torsion points in terms of the modular lambda function and its associated elliptic polynomial, resulting in a parameterized family of genus-one curves with rational points. This approach allows us to recover and extend previous findings, as well as uncover new results, including the confirmation of invariants' independence from the computation method used. Our proof also yields previously unknown rational points and birational families of points for certain genus-one curves.

Our research delves into the impact of complex top squark and stop phase angles on the production of heavy Higgs bosons in top squark-associated processes at the Large Hadron Collider. We examine the contributions of top squarks and stops to the heavy Higgs boson production cross-sections for complex parameters ranging from 0 to $\pi/2$. Our analysis reveals that the effects of top squark and stop phases on the production cross-sections of heavy Higgs bosons are most pronounced in the scalar phase angle and diminish as the fermion phase angle increases. Furthermore, we found that the effects of complex top squark and stop phases on the production cross-sections of heavy Higgs bosons can be detected through precise measurements of the total cross-sections of top squark-associated heavy Higgs boson production.

In the realm of contextual linear bandits, an agent learns to minimize regret by making contextual decisions and receiving outcomes over time. A key issue involves designing an efficient communication protocol between the agent and a learner to exchange the decision and outcome data. This paper presents a novel approach to analyzing the relationship between the learner's knowledge of the context distribution and the cost of communication. Specifically, it demonstrates that if the context distribution's underlying knowledge is accessible to both parties, communication can be minimized to $d$ bits per round. Conversely, if the context distribution's knowledge is unknown to the learner but accessible to the agent, the cost of communication increases to $d+\sqrt{T}$ bits. This result is further supported by a lower bound of $\Omega(d+\sqrt{T})$ bits, establishing the optimality of the proposed approach.

In offline reinforcement learning, out-of-distribution data can lead to unreliable value function estimates, particularly in large state-action spaces where random behavior often fails to visit all states effectively. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach to evaluate value function estimates using only on-policy data, thereby avoiding the problem of using unreliable estimates for off-state actions. Our method iteratively refines the policy by adopting actions with high-confidence value function estimates, effectively filtering out data with unreliable estimates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in offline settings by combining it with existing techniques, resulting in a significant reduction in testing sample size required to achieve optimal performance compared to standard methods. Our findings indicate that our proposed approach can substantially decrease the testing sample size required to achieve equivalent performance to conventional methods.

The transverse momentum distributions of charged hadrons, specifically pions, protons, and kaons, were measured in 20 to 80% of central oxygen-gold collisions at a collision energy of 7.2 GeV. These distributions were found to widen significantly as the transverse momentum increased for both pion and proton species. A fit using a Boltzmann model yielded a temperature of approximately 105 MeV, which is notably higher than the chemical freeze-out temperature predicted by the Coalescence and Hadronization Dynamics model. The ratio of protons to pions matched the ratio predicted by the Coalescence and Hadronization Dynamics model, while the ratio of positive to negative pions was found to be greater than one at low transverse momentum.
